analysis.one_liner: Restores union organizing rights: card-check certification, binding first contracts, public-employee bargaining, and employer penalties.
analysis.headline: The Workplace Democracy Act of 1999 was referred to committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal labor law to make it much easier for workers to form unions and win contracts. Employers would have had to recognize a union once a majority of workers signed cards, a union stuck without a first contract could force binding arbitration, penalties for firing organizers would rise sharply, and public employees nationwide would gain collective bargaining rights for the first time. It also would have applied U.S. labor law to American companies' operations abroad and put workers on the boards overseeing their pensions.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize unions, and unions themselves. Card-check certification would remove the long, employer-contested election process where workers can be fired or pressured before a vote. The first-contract arbitration rule addresses the common tactic where an employer simply refuses to agree to any contract after a union wins. Employees fired for organizing would be reinstated immediately pending review, wrongfully fired workers or injured third parties could recover triple damages, and willful violators could be barred from federal contracts and hit with $10,000 penalties per violation. Public employees in states without bargaining laws would gain the right to organize and strike, and pension participants would win seats on the boards running their plans.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must certify a union as soon as a majority of workers in a unit sign recognition cards, bypassing the National Labor Relations Board election process.

If no collective bargaining agreement is reached within 45 days of certification, the union can send the contract dispute to compulsory and binding arbitration, so employers cannot stall a first contract indefinitely.

Employers must reinstate a discharged worker once an unfair labor practice complaint is issued, and the Board must seek injunctions and assess civil penalties of at least $10,000 per willful violation.
Workers or others financially injured by discriminatory firings can sue in federal court for triple damages, with a Board violation ruling treated as prima facie evidence.
Willful violators can be debarred from federal contracts for up to three years.

Public employees gain a federal right to form unions, bargain collectively, and strike, enforced by a new National Public Employment Relations Commission, overriding state laws that deny those rights.

The National Labor Relations Act would apply to U.S. companies and their subsidiaries in countries with a U.S. free trade agreement, letting those workers file unfair labor practice complaints against the American parent.
Single-employer pension plans must be run by a joint board of trustees with equal representation for participants and beneficiaries.

The bill repeals the section of federal law that lets states ban union security agreements, so workers could no longer be required to pay union fees where right-to-work laws now apply; it also repeals bans on secondary strikes, boycotts, and hot cargo agreements, restoring tools unions lost under the Taft-Hartley Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who contest union organizing, including retail, manufacturing, and service companies with large non-union workforces, would face faster certification, binding contract terms from an arbitrator, real penalties, reinstatement of fired organizers, treble-damage lawsuits, and possible loss of federal contracts. State and local governments would become mandatory collective bargaining employers, with arbitration awards binding on legislative bodies, and taxpayers could bear higher public payrolls. American multinationals would face U.S. labor law enforcement at their overseas operations.

drawbacks.text: Card-check certification replaces the secret-ballot election with signed cards collected by union organizers, which critics argue exposes workers to union-side pressure just as elections expose them to employer pressure.
Binding arbitration can impose a first contract, or an award binding on a state legislature, on an employer that never agreed to its terms, raising public budgets and private labor costs.
Repealing the secondary boycott and hot cargo prohibitions would again allow union pressure campaigns directed at neutral customers and suppliers of a target employer.
Repealing the state right-to-work provision overrides the union-security laws of every state that has enacted them, which supporters of those laws view as an individual choice issue.
Allowing public employee strikes, with limits, and mandatory bargaining could disrupt public services while arbitration resolves disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core premise — that workers' rights to organize are hard to exercise under current law — is a long-standing finding of labor law scholars, and its mechanisms target the well-documented gaps: delay tactics before elections and refusal to bargain a first contract. But it goes far beyond incremental fixes, simultaneously upending certification, contract formation, strike law, right-to-work, public-sector bargaining, and extraterritorial application. The breadth, not the goal, is what made it politically impossible; even labor-friendly members did not sign on, and a version passed only much later in far narrower form. As written, it was a maximalist rewrite whose costs to employers, governments, and taxpayers were never seriously examined because no hearing ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and then sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and not one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, introduced the bill on March 24, 1999.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 30, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where no further action was taken.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced card-check certification, compulsory first-contract arbitration, $10,000 per-violation penalties, treble-damage suits, and federal contract debarment are better off because the bill never advanced; workers who might have organized under the new rules gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and gave it its maximalist labor-law design.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup on it; referred it to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it died.

against.name: Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after the April 30, 1999 referral and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House majority (Republican)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration, and no Republican signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the only sponsor was an Independent, so no party split can be measured; the absence of a single cosponsor from either party shows the bill had no organized floor support.

industries.note: Card-check certification and compulsory first-contract arbitration would remove the election delay and the refuse-to-bargain strategies such employers rely on, and willful violators would face $10,000 penalties, treble-damage suits, and debarment from federal contracts. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against workers seeking union representation.
Willful labor law violators could be barred from federal contracts for up to three years, a sanction that did not previously exist in this form.

All public employers would become mandatory bargaining units under a new federal commission, with arbitration awards binding even on legislative bodies and strikes permitted except for firefighters and public safety officers — shifting costs onto taxpayers.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational companies with operations in free-trade-agreement countries
industries.note: The National Labor Relations Act would follow American companies abroad, and workers at their foreign subsidiaries could file unfair labor practice complaints against the U.S. parent.

Certification by signed cards, guaranteed first contracts, restored secondary boycott rights, union security enforcement, and new public-sector members would all expand union membership and bargaining power — the same outcomes workers exercising their right to organize would gain.

Single-employer pension plans would be required to add participant- or union-designated trustees with equal voting power, giving retirement savers a say in how their money is managed; existing employer-appointed trustees would lose sole control.
